TITLE: AI Training vs Inference: What's the Difference (and Why It Matters for Hardware)
LABEL: GUIDE
EXCERPT: Training teaches an AI model by adjusting billions of parameters; inference uses the finished model to answer requests. How the two differ in compute, memory, cost and hardware, with simple formulas and real numbers.
KEY: Training is when an AI model learns: it processes huge datasets and repeatedly adjusts its parameters to reduce errors. Inference is when the finished model is used: it takes a new input, such as your prompt, and produces an output without changing its parameters. Training is a huge one-off job (roughly 6 FLOPs per parameter per token) that needs large GPU clusters; inference costs about 2 FLOPs per parameter per token but runs millions of times a day, so over a model's life it often costs more in total.
content:
Short answer

Training is when an AI model learns: it processes huge datasets and repeatedly adjusts its parameters to reduce errors. Inference is when the finished model is used: it takes a new input, such as your prompt, and produces an output without changing its parameters. Training is a huge one-off job (roughly 6 FLOPs per parameter per token) that needs large GPU clusters; inference costs about 2 FLOPs per parameter per token but runs millions of times a day, so over a model's life it often costs more in total.

The simple version

Think of a student. Training is studying for years: reading textbooks, doing exercises, getting corrected and improving. Inference is sitting the exam: using what was learned to answer new questions quickly, without learning anything new during the exam.

For an AI model:

  • Training = forward pass + measuring the error (loss) + backward pass (backpropagation) + updating the weights. Repeated over billions or trillions of examples.
  • Inference = forward pass only. Input goes in, output comes out, weights stay fixed.

Side-by-side comparison

Why training needs so much compute

A widely used rule of thumb is that training a transformer takes about 6 × N × D floating-point operations, where N is the number of parameters and D is the number of training tokens. The forward pass costs about 2N per token and the backward pass about twice that.

Real examples:

  • GPT-3 (175 billion parameters) was trained on about 300 billion tokens, roughly 3.14 × 10²³ FLOPs according to its paper.
  • Llama 3.1 405B was trained on about 15.6 trillion tokens with about 3.8 × 10²⁵ FLOPs, using up to 16,000 NVIDIA H100 GPUs.

That is why training happens in GPU clusters inside AI data centers, and why the cost of a frontier training run reaches tens or hundreds of millions of dollars. Our LLM training cost guide breaks down the maths.

Why training needs so much memory

During training, each parameter needs more than its weight in memory. With standard mixed-precision training and the Adam optimizer you store:

  • FP16/BF16 weights: 2 bytes
  • FP16/BF16 gradients: 2 bytes
  • FP32 master copy of the weights: 4 bytes
  • Adam optimizer states (two FP32 values): 8 bytes

That is about 16 bytes per parameter before activations. A 7-billion-parameter model therefore needs around 112 GB just for these states, more than a single 80 GB H100 holds. Large models are split across many GPUs using data, tensor, pipeline and optimizer-state parallelism, which is why fast interconnects such as NVLink and NVSwitch matter so much. See mixed precision training for the details.

For inference, the same 7B model needs only about 14 GB in FP16, or around 4 to 5 GB when quantized to 4 bits (see LLM quantization).

Why inference is limited by memory bandwidth

When a language model generates text, it produces one token at a time. For every token, the GPU has to read essentially all of the model's weights from memory. With small batches, the GPU spends more time waiting for data than calculating, so speed depends on memory bandwidth, not peak TFLOPS.

Inference also has two phases with different behaviour, explained in prefill vs decode:

  • Prefill processes your whole prompt at once and is compute-bound.
  • Decode generates the answer token by token and is memory-bound.

Serving many users adds the KV cache, which grows with every token of context and can take more memory than the weights themselves. You can see these effects in our LLM inference simulator.

Which costs more overall?

Training is a large, one-off bill. Inference is a smaller cost per request, multiplied by every user and every request for as long as the model is in service. For popular AI products, cumulative inference spending can exceed the training cost. This is why chipmakers are designing inference-specific hardware, such as Google's Ironwood TPU and the Groq LPU, and why NVIDIA promotes low-precision formats like NVFP4 for serving.

Newer reasoning models make inference even more important: they generate thousands of hidden "thinking" tokens before answering, so each request uses far more compute than a normal chatbot reply.

Hardware for training vs inference

If you only need occasional training or fine-tuning, renting is usually cheaper than buying; compare current rates in our GPU cloud price tracker and read rent vs buy a GPU.

Frequently asked questions

Does a model learn during inference?

No. During normal inference the weights are frozen. A chatbot can "remember" earlier messages only because they are included in its context window, not because it updated its parameters.

Is fine-tuning training or inference?

Fine-tuning is training: it runs forward and backward passes and updates weights, just on a smaller dataset and usually for far fewer steps. See What is fine-tuning?.

Can I use the same GPU for training and inference?

Yes. Any modern NVIDIA GPU with tensor cores can do both. Training simply needs much more memory, so a card that runs a 13B model comfortably may only be able to fine-tune a 7B model with memory-saving tricks.

Why is inference called "inference"?

The term comes from statistics, where inference means drawing conclusions from data with a fitted model. In AI it simply means running a trained model on new inputs.

Sources and further reading

  • Kaplan et al., Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models (2020)
  • Brown et al., Language Models are Few-Shot Learners (GPT-3, 2020)
  • Rajbhandari et al., ZeRO: Memory Optimizations Toward Training Trillion Parameter Models (2019)
  • Meta, The Llama 3 Herd of Models (2024)

TITLE: Best GPU for Stable Diffusion and FLUX in 2026: How Much VRAM You Really Need
LABEL: BUYING GUIDE
EXCERPT: Which graphics card should you buy for Stable Diffusion, SDXL, FLUX and AI video? VRAM requirements by model, our picks from budget to high end, NVIDIA vs AMD vs Mac, and when renting a cloud GPU makes more sense.
KEY: For local AI image generation, VRAM matters more than anything else. 16 GB is the sweet spot in 2026: it runs SDXL comfortably and FLUX with FP8 or GGUF quantized weights. The RTX 5060 Ti 16 GB is the best budget pick, the RTX 5070 Ti 16 GB the best value for speed, and the RTX 5090 32 GB the best overall, especially for full-precision FLUX and AI video. A used RTX 3090 24 GB is a strong value alternative. NVIDIA remains the easiest choice because nearly every tool is built on CUDA.
content:
Short answer

For local AI image generation, VRAM matters more than anything else. 16 GB is the sweet spot in 2026: it runs SDXL comfortably and FLUX with FP8 or GGUF quantized weights. The RTX 5060 Ti 16 GB is the best budget pick, the RTX 5070 Ti 16 GB the best value for speed, and the RTX 5090 32 GB the best overall, especially for full-precision FLUX and AI video. A used RTX 3090 24 GB is a strong value alternative. NVIDIA remains the easiest choice because nearly every tool is built on CUDA.

Why VRAM is the most important spec

Image models must hold their weights, the text encoders, the image decoder (VAE) and working data in GPU memory. If they do not fit, tools fall back to offloading parts to system RAM, which can make generation many times slower, or they fail with an "out of memory" error.

More VRAM also lets you:

  • Generate at higher resolutions and in larger batches
  • Use ControlNet, IP-Adapter and LoRAs at the same time
  • Train your own LoRAs
  • Run newer, larger models at full quality
  • Generate AI video, which needs far more memory than still images

For a deeper explanation, see What is VRAM?.

How much VRAM each model needs

Approximate comfortable VRAM for generating 1024×1024 images in popular tools like ComfyUI or Forge. Memory-saving options can go lower at the cost of speed.

Quantization shrinks models with a small loss of quality; the same ideas apply as for LLM quantization.

Our GPU picks

Prices below are NVIDIA's and AMD's US launch prices. Street prices in 2026 are often higher because of memory shortages and AI demand (see why GPU prices are rising), so compare current offers before buying.

Best overall: RTX 5090 (32 GB)

The fastest consumer GPU for AI image generation, with 32 GB of fast GDDR7 and about 1.8 TB/s of memory bandwidth. It runs FLUX at full precision with room for ControlNets and LoRAs, handles larger AI video models and trains LoRAs quickly. Its fifth-generation tensor cores support FP4 for even faster quantized inference. It draws up to 575 W, so check your power supply. Full analysis: Is the RTX 5090 good for AI?.

Best value for VRAM: used RTX 3090 (24 GB)

Older and slower than current cards, but 24 GB of VRAM at used prices makes it a favourite for FLUX, video models and LoRA training. Check the card's condition, cooling and warranty, and expect high power draw.

Best value for speed: RTX 5070 Ti (16 GB)

Fast Blackwell architecture with 16 GB of GDDR7. It handles SDXL quickly and FLUX in FP8 or GGUF formats, which is what most people use day to day.

Best budget: RTX 5060 Ti 16 GB

Make sure you buy the 16 GB version, not the 8 GB one. It is slower than the 5070 Ti, but the extra memory means it can run the same models, just taking longer per image. It is the cheapest new card we recommend for FLUX.

Avoid for AI image work

  • 8 GB cards (RTX 5060, RTX 4060, 5060 Ti 8 GB): fine for SD 1.5, tight for SDXL and very limited for FLUX and video.
  • RTX 5070 (12 GB): fast, but 12 GB limits newer models. A 16 GB card is a better buy for AI.

NVIDIA vs AMD vs Apple vs Intel

  • NVIDIA: the default. ComfyUI, Forge, Automatic1111, kohya_ss and nearly all custom nodes are developed and tested on CUDA first.
  • AMD: works with ROCm on Linux and increasingly on Windows, but setup is harder, some extensions do not work and performance per dollar is often lower for AI. See AMD vs NVIDIA for AI.
  • Apple Silicon Macs: run Stable Diffusion and FLUX through apps like Draw Things or ComfyUI with Metal. Large unified memory helps fit big models, but generation is usually much slower than a high-end NVIDIA GPU.
  • Intel Arc: works with some tools, but software support is the most limited.

Other parts of your PC

  • System RAM: 32 GB minimum, 64 GB recommended for FLUX and video workflows.
  • Storage: a fast NVMe SSD with plenty of space; model files are often 5 to 25 GB each.
  • Power supply: follow the GPU maker's recommendation (1,000 W for an RTX 5090).

Should you rent a cloud GPU instead?

If you generate images only occasionally, or want to try large video models before buying, renting can be cheaper. Consumer cards like the RTX 4090 and 5090 rent for well under a dollar an hour on some GPU marketplaces, and data center GPUs such as the H100 are available by the hour. Compare live prices in our GPU cloud price tracker, and see rent vs buy a GPU and cheapest cloud GPU.

Frequently asked questions

Can I run Stable Diffusion on 8 GB of VRAM?

Yes for SD 1.5 and SDXL with memory-saving settings, and FLUX with heavily quantized GGUF models, but it will be slower and more limited. If you are buying a GPU for AI, choose 16 GB or more.

Is the RTX 5090 worth it over the 5080 for Stable Diffusion?

If you want full-precision FLUX, AI video or fast LoRA training, yes: the jump from 16 GB to 32 GB matters more than raw speed. For SDXL and quantized FLUX only, the 5080 or 5070 Ti is much better value.

Does Stable Diffusion use tensor cores?

Yes. Image generation is dominated by matrix multiplications in FP16, BF16 and FP8, which run on tensor cores. See tensor cores vs CUDA cores.

Is the same GPU good for local LLMs?

Mostly yes. Both workloads reward VRAM and memory bandwidth. Our best GPU for local LLMs guide covers language models specifically.

Sources and further reading

  • NVIDIA, GeForce RTX 5090 specifications
  • Black Forest Labs, FLUX.1 dev on Hugging Face
  • Stability AI, Stable Diffusion 3.5 Large on Hugging Face
  • Podell et al., SDXL: Improving Latent Diffusion Models for High-Resolution Image Synthesis (2023)
  • ComfyUI, GitHub repository

TITLE: How Does ChatGPT Work? A Simple Step-by-Step Explanation
LABEL: GUIDE
EXCERPT: ChatGPT works by predicting the next token with a huge transformer model that was pre-trained on internet-scale text and then tuned with human feedback. A plain-English walkthrough of what happens from training to the moment you press Enter, including reasoning, tools and the GPUs behind it.
KEY: ChatGPT works by repeatedly predicting the next token (a word or part of a word) using a very large transformer neural network. That model was first pre-trained on a vast amount of text to learn language and knowledge, then fine-tuned on example conversations and with reinforcement learning from human feedback to become a helpful assistant. When you send a message, your text is split into tokens, processed on GPUs in a data center, and the reply is generated one token at a time. Tools such as web search and code execution let it look things up and calculate instead of guessing.
content:
Short answer

ChatGPT works by repeatedly predicting the next token (a word or part of a word) using a very large transformer neural network. That model was first pre-trained on a vast amount of text to learn language and knowledge, then fine-tuned on example conversations and with reinforcement learning from human feedback to become a helpful assistant. When you send a message, your text is split into tokens, processed on GPUs in a data center, and the reply is generated one token at a time. Tools such as web search and code execution let it look things up and calculate instead of guessing.

The short version

1. Pre-training: a GPT model reads an enormous amount of text and learns to predict the next token. 2. Fine-tuning: it is trained on example conversations written or rated by people. 3. Reinforcement learning: it is rewarded for answers people prefer and for correct solutions. 4. Your message: your text plus the conversation so far is turned into tokens. 5. Generation: the model predicts the reply token by token, running on GPUs. 6. Extras: search, file reading, code execution, memory and image generation are tools around the model.

Step 1: Pre-training, learning from text

ChatGPT is powered by OpenAI's GPT family of large language models. "GPT" stands for Generative Pre-trained Transformer.

During pre-training, the model is shown huge amounts of text from public web pages, books, code and licensed data. Its task is simple: given the text so far, predict the next token. Every time it predicts wrongly, the training algorithm adjusts its billions of parameters slightly to make the correct token more likely next time.

Repeated over trillions of tokens, this teaches the model grammar, facts, writing styles, reasoning patterns and programming. GPT-3, released in 2020, had 175 billion parameters; OpenAI has not published the sizes of its later models. Pre-training a frontier model takes thousands of GPUs running for months. See AI training vs inference for what that involves.

After pre-training, the model is a powerful text completer, but not yet a good assistant. Ask it a question and it might continue with more questions.

Step 2: Supervised fine-tuning

Next, the model is fine-tuned on example conversations: prompts paired with high-quality answers. This teaches it the format of a helpful dialogue: answer the question, follow instructions, ask for clarification when needed.

Step 3: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF)

OpenAI described this approach in its 2022 InstructGPT paper, the forerunner of ChatGPT:

1. The model writes several answers to the same prompt. 2. Human reviewers rank the answers from best to worst. 3. A separate reward model learns to predict which answers people prefer. 4. The language model is then trained with reinforcement learning to produce answers the reward model scores highly.

This is a big part of why ChatGPT is polite, follows instructions and declines some harmful requests. It is also part of the AI alignment effort to make models behave as intended.

Step 4: What happens when you press Enter

1. Context building: the app combines a hidden system prompt, any memory or custom instructions, the conversation so far, uploaded files and your new message. 2. Tokenization: all of that text is split into tokens and converted to numbers. The total must fit inside the model's context window. 3. Prefill: the whole input is processed in one pass on GPUs. The model builds an internal representation of every token using attention, which lets each token draw information from all the others, and stores the results in a KV cache. 4. Decoding: the model outputs a probability for every possible next token. One is chosen (with some randomness controlled by settings like temperature), appended to the text, and the process repeats. That is why replies stream onto your screen word by word. Try it in our LLM sampling simulator. 5. Stopping: generation ends when the model produces a special end token or hits a length limit.

The model does not search a database of stored answers. Each reply is generated fresh, which is why asking the same question twice can give different wording.

Reasoning models: thinking before answering

Starting with OpenAI's o1 in September 2024, some models are trained with reinforcement learning to produce a long internal chain of reasoning before giving a final answer. They are rewarded for reaching correct solutions on maths, coding and logic problems. In ChatGPT, these models may show a summary of their "thinking". The reasoning tokens cost extra compute, so these answers are slower but usually more accurate on hard problems.

Tools: search, code and more

On its own, a language model only knows what was in its training data, up to a knowledge cut-off date, and it can make up facts (hallucinate). ChatGPT reduces this with tools the model can decide to call:

  • Web search: fetches current pages and cites them.
  • Code execution: runs Python to analyse data or do exact calculations.
  • File reading: extracts text from PDFs, spreadsheets and documents, similar to RAG.
  • Image generation and vision: creates images and understands uploaded photos.
  • Agent features: can browse and take multi-step actions, as described in What is an AI agent?.

The hardware behind ChatGPT

Every message runs on large clusters of NVIDIA GPUs in AI data centers operated by OpenAI and cloud partners such as Microsoft Azure. A large model is split across several GPUs connected by NVLink, and requests from many users are batched together so each GPU stays busy. The speed of each reply depends mostly on GPU memory bandwidth, because generating each token requires reading the model's weights. Serving hundreds of millions of weekly users is why OpenAI has signed some of the largest compute deals in history.

What ChatGPT is not

  • It is not a search engine, unless it is using its search tool.
  • It is not conscious and does not have goals of its own.
  • It does not learn from your chat in real time. Conversations can be used to improve future models depending on your settings, but the model's weights do not change during your chat.
  • It is not always right. Check important facts, figures and citations.

Frequently asked questions

Does ChatGPT copy answers from the internet?

No. It generates new text from patterns learned during training. It can repeat common phrases or well-known passages, and when it uses web search it summarises and cites the pages it found.

Why does ChatGPT make mistakes?

Because it predicts plausible text rather than checking facts, it can produce confident errors. Gaps in training data, ambiguous questions and its knowledge cut-off all contribute. See AI hallucinations.

How does ChatGPT remember earlier messages?

The whole conversation is sent to the model again with each new message, inside its context window. Very long chats may be trimmed or summarised.

Can I run ChatGPT on my own computer?

Not ChatGPT itself, but you can run open models with similar abilities, including OpenAI's open-weight gpt-oss models, on your own hardware. See how to run an LLM locally and the best GPU for local LLMs.

Sources and further reading

  • Radford et al., Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training (GPT-1, 2018)
  • Brown et al., Language Models are Few-Shot Learners (GPT-3, 2020)
  • Ouyang et al., Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback (2022)
  • OpenAI, Introducing ChatGPT (2022)
  • OpenAI, Learning to reason with LLMs (2024)

TITLE: What Are Embeddings in AI? Vectors, Semantic Search and Vector Databases Explained
LABEL: GUIDE
EXCERPT: Embeddings turn words, documents and images into lists of numbers that capture meaning, so computers can find similar things. How embeddings work, cosine similarity, vector databases, how RAG uses them, and how much memory they need.
KEY: An embedding is a list of numbers (a vector) that represents the meaning of a piece of data such as a word, sentence, document, image or product. Embedding models are trained so that similar things get similar vectors, which lets computers find related content by comparing numbers instead of matching exact keywords. Embeddings power semantic search, recommendations, clustering and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and they are usually stored and searched in a vector database.
content:
Short answer

An embedding is a list of numbers (a vector) that represents the meaning of a piece of data such as a word, sentence, document, image or product. Embedding models are trained so that similar things get similar vectors, which lets computers find related content by comparing numbers instead of matching exact keywords. Embeddings power semantic search, recommendations, clustering and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and they are usually stored and searched in a vector database.

The idea: meaning as coordinates

Imagine placing every word on a map so that words with similar meanings sit close together: "cat" near "kitten", "GPU" near "graphics card", "Paris" near "France". An embedding is a position on such a map, except the map has hundreds or thousands of dimensions instead of two.

For example, a sentence might become a vector like this (shortened):

"How much VRAM do I need for Llama?"  →  [0.021, -0.113, 0.087, ..., 0.045]   (1,536 numbers)

The individual numbers have no simple human meaning. What matters is how close vectors are to each other.

Measuring similarity

The most common measure is cosine similarity, which compares the angle between two vectors:

  • Close to 1: very similar meaning
  • Around 0: unrelated
  • Negative: opposite in some sense (rare in practice for text embeddings)

Other measures are dot product and Euclidean (L2) distance. Many embedding models output normalised vectors, in which case cosine similarity and dot product give the same ranking.

Where embeddings come from

Embeddings are produced by neural networks trained so that related items end up close together:

  • Word2vec (2013) learned word vectors by predicting nearby words. It became famous for vector arithmetic such as king − man + woman ≈ queen.
  • Transformer encoders such as BERT and Sentence-BERT produce embeddings for whole sentences and paragraphs, taking context into account, so "bank" in "river bank" and "bank account" get different representations.
  • Modern embedding models from OpenAI, Google, Cohere, Voyage and open-source projects (such as the BGE, E5, GTE, Nomic and Qwen embedding families) are trained on huge sets of matching pairs, like questions and their answers.
  • Multimodal models such as CLIP place images and text in the same space, so the text "a red sports car" lands near photos of red sports cars.

Inside every large language model, the first step is also an embedding: each token ID is turned into a vector before the transformer layers process it.

What embeddings are used for

  • Semantic search: find documents that match the meaning of a query, even without the same words. A search for "GPU running out of memory" can find a page titled "Fixing CUDA OOM errors".
  • RAG: retrieve the most relevant passages and give them to a chatbot so it answers from real sources, reducing hallucinations.
  • Recommendations: suggest products, articles or songs similar to ones a user liked.
  • Clustering and topic discovery: group support tickets, reviews or articles by theme.
  • Duplicate detection: find near-identical questions or pages.
  • Classification: use embeddings as input features for a small, fast classifier.
  • Anomaly detection: flag items whose vectors are far from everything else.

How embeddings power RAG, step by step

1. Chunk your documents into passages of a few hundred tokens. 2. Embed every chunk with an embedding model and store the vectors with the original text. 3. When a user asks a question, embed the question with the same model. 4. Search for the chunks whose vectors are most similar to the question vector. 5. Insert the top results into the language model's context window and ask it to answer using them, with citations.

Many systems combine vector search with traditional keyword search (hybrid search) and re-rank the results with a second model for better accuracy. For the full picture see What is RAG?.

Vector databases

Comparing a query against millions of vectors one by one is slow, so vector databases use approximate nearest neighbour (ANN) indexes, such as HNSW graphs or IVF clustering, that find very close matches in milliseconds while checking only a small fraction of vectors.

Popular options:

How much memory do embeddings need?

Storage is simple to estimate: number of vectors × dimensions × bytes per number.

Indexes add overhead on top. Common ways to cut costs:

  • Fewer dimensions: some models, including OpenAI's text-embedding-3 models, let you shorten vectors with only a small loss of accuracy.
  • Quantization: store vectors as INT8 or binary, the same idea as model quantization.
  • GPU acceleration: libraries such as FAISS and NVIDIA cuVS can build and search indexes on GPUs, which helps with very large collections.

Creating embeddings for millions of documents is also a good fit for GPUs, because embedding models are small and process text in large parallel batches.

How to choose an embedding model

  • Check benchmarks like the MTEB leaderboard on Hugging Face, but test on your own data.
  • Match your languages: use a multilingual model if your content is not only in English.
  • Consider dimensions and cost: larger vectors can be more accurate but cost more to store and search.
  • Check the maximum input length so your chunks fit.
  • Never mix models: queries and documents must be embedded with the same model. Changing models means re-embedding everything.

Frequently asked questions

Are embeddings the same as tokens?

No. Tokens are the pieces text is split into, each with an ID number. Embeddings are dense vectors of many numbers that represent meaning. Language models convert tokens into embeddings as their first step.

What is the difference between a vector and an embedding?

A vector is any list of numbers. An embedding is a vector produced by a model specifically to represent the meaning or features of some data.

Do I need a vector database?

Not always. For a few thousand documents, an in-memory array or pgvector in an existing database is enough. Dedicated vector databases help when you have millions of vectors, need filtering at scale or want managed infrastructure.

Can embeddings work for images and audio?

Yes. Image, audio and multimodal embedding models place these data types in vector spaces too, enabling reverse image search, finding similar sounds and searching photos with text.

Sources and further reading

  • Mikolov et al., Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space (word2vec, 2013)
  • Reimers and Gurevych, Sentence-BERT (2019)
  • Radford et al., Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision (CLIP, 2021)
  • Malkov and Yashunin, HNSW graphs for approximate nearest neighbor search (2016)
  • Hugging Face, MTEB leaderboard

TITLE: What Are Tokens in AI? How LLMs Read Text, Count Words and Charge You
LABEL: GUIDE
EXCERPT: Tokens are the small chunks of text that language models read and write. What a token is, how tokenizers work, how many words are in 1,000 tokens, why tokens decide API prices, context limits and speed, and how to count them.
KEY: A token is the basic unit of text a language model reads and writes. It can be a whole word, part of a word, a punctuation mark or a space. In English, one token is on average about 4 characters or three quarters of a word, so 1,000 tokens ≈ 750 words. Tokens matter because AI APIs charge per token, context windows are measured in tokens, and generation speed is measured in tokens per second.
content:
Short answer

A token is the basic unit of text a language model reads and writes. It can be a whole word, part of a word, a punctuation mark or a space. In English, one token is on average about 4 characters or three quarters of a word, so 1,000 tokens ≈ 750 words. Tokens matter because AI APIs charge per token, context windows are measured in tokens, and generation speed is measured in tokens per second.

Why AI models use tokens

Neural networks only work with numbers. Before a large language model can process your prompt, a tokenizer splits the text into tokens and replaces each one with an integer ID from a fixed vocabulary. The model then works on those IDs, and its output IDs are turned back into text.

Why not just use whole words or single characters?

  • Whole words would need a gigantic vocabulary and could not handle new words, typos or names.
  • Single characters make sequences very long, which makes models slower and more expensive, because attention cost grows with sequence length.
  • Subword tokens are the compromise: common words get one token, rare words are split into pieces.

A tokenization example

The sentence "Tensor cores accelerate unbelievably large matrix multiplications." might be split like this (exact splits vary by tokenizer):

Tensor | cores | accelerate | unbel | iev | ably | large | matrix | multip | lications | .

Common words such as "large" and "matrix" are single tokens. The rare word "unbelievably" is broken into three pieces. A leading space is usually part of the token, so " cores" and "cores" can have different IDs.

How tokenizers are built

Most modern LLMs use a variant of byte pair encoding (BPE):

1. Start with individual bytes or characters. 2. Find the pair of symbols that appears most often in a large text corpus and merge it into a new symbol. 3. Repeat thousands of times until the vocabulary reaches the target size.

The result is a vocabulary where frequent strings ("the", "ing", " model") are single tokens. Other common methods are WordPiece (used by BERT) and SentencePiece/Unigram (used by many multilingual models).

Vocabulary sizes have grown over time: Llama 3 uses about 128,000 tokens and OpenAI's GPT-4o tokenizer (o200k_base) about 200,000. Larger vocabularies make text shorter in tokens, especially for non-English languages and code.

How many words is a token?

OpenAI's rule of thumb for English:

Other languages usually need more tokens for the same meaning. Languages with non-Latin scripts, such as Hindi, Urdu, Arabic, Thai or Burmese, can need two to several times more tokens than English, which makes them slower and more expensive on some models. Code also tokenizes less efficiently than prose because of spaces, symbols and indentation.

Why tokens matter

1. Price

AI APIs charge per million tokens, with separate prices for input tokens (your prompt, documents and chat history) and output tokens (the model's reply). Output tokens usually cost several times more because they are generated one at a time. Long chat histories get expensive because the whole conversation is sent again with every message. Reasoning models also bill for hidden "thinking" tokens.

2. Context window

A model's context window is its maximum number of tokens for the prompt plus the response. If a conversation or document exceeds it, older content must be cut or summarised.

3. Speed

Generation speed is measured in tokens per second. Each output token requires reading the model's weights from memory, so speed depends heavily on GPU memory bandwidth. Two numbers matter: time to first token (how long before the reply starts, driven by prefill) and tokens per second during generation.

4. Memory

Every token in the context adds to the KV cache stored in GPU memory. That is why very long prompts need much more VRAM.

Why tokens explain some odd AI mistakes

Because models see tokens, not letters, they can struggle with tasks that need character-level detail:

  • Counting letters ("how many r's in strawberry?") is hard when the word is one or two tokens.
  • Spelling backwards, rhymes and anagrams are harder than they look.
  • Arithmetic on long numbers can suffer when digits are grouped into tokens in inconsistent ways.

Newer models handle many of these cases better, often by reasoning step by step or by using a code tool.

How to count tokens

  • OpenAI Tokenizer (web tool) shows exactly how text is split for OpenAI models.
  • tiktoken (Python) counts tokens for OpenAI models in code:
import tiktoken
enc = tiktoken.get_encoding("o200k_base")
print(len(enc.encode("How many tokens is this sentence?")))
  • Hugging Face tokenizers load the exact tokenizer for open models such as Llama, Mistral or Qwen with AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(...).
  • Most API responses also report the input and output token counts used.

How sampling picks the next token

At each step the model outputs a probability for every token in its vocabulary. Settings such as temperature, top-k and top-p decide how the next token is chosen from those probabilities. You can experiment with this in our LLM sampling simulator.

Frequently asked questions

Is a token the same as a word?

No. Short common words are often one token, but longer or rarer words are split into several. On average an English word is about 1.3 tokens.

Do images and audio use tokens?

Yes. Multimodal models convert images into patches and audio into short segments, each represented as tokens. A single image can use hundreds or more than a thousand tokens, depending on its resolution and the model.

Are tokens the same across models?

No. Each model family has its own tokenizer, so the same text can be a different number of tokens on GPT, Claude, Gemini and Llama. Always count with the tokenizer of the model you use.

Why do output tokens cost more than input tokens?

Input tokens are processed in parallel in one pass, which uses the GPU efficiently. Output tokens are generated one at a time, and each step reads the full model from memory, so they use much more GPU time per token.

Sources and further reading

  • Sennrich et al., Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units (BPE, 2015)
  • OpenAI, Tokenizer tool
  • OpenAI, tiktoken on GitHub
  • Hugging Face, Summary of the tokenizers

TITLE: What Is a Context Window in AI? Limits, Memory Cost and Why Bigger Isn't Always Better
LABEL: GUIDE
EXCERPT: A context window is the maximum amount of text, measured in tokens, that an AI model can consider at once. What it includes, typical sizes, why long context needs so much GPU memory, the "lost in the middle" problem and practical tips.
KEY: A context window is the maximum number of tokens a language model can take into account at one time: your prompt, any documents or chat history, system instructions and the model's own reply together. It works like the model's short-term working memory. Context windows have grown from about 2,000 tokens in GPT-3 to 128,000 tokens to over 1 million in many current models, but long contexts need a lot of GPU memory and models do not use every part of a long context equally well.
content:
Short answer

A context window is the maximum number of tokens a language model can take into account at one time: your prompt, any documents or chat history, system instructions and the model's own reply together. It works like the model's short-term working memory. Context windows have grown from about 2,000 tokens in GPT-3 to 128,000 tokens to over 1 million in many current models, but long contexts need a lot of GPU memory and models do not use every part of a long context equally well.

What goes into the context window

Everything the model "sees" for a single response counts against the limit:

  • System prompt: the hidden instructions that set the assistant's behaviour.
  • Conversation history: every previous message in the chat.
  • Documents and tool results: pasted text, uploaded files, search results or RAG snippets.
  • Your current prompt.
  • The model's output: the reply, plus any hidden reasoning tokens for reasoning models.

When a conversation grows beyond the window, the application must drop or summarise older messages. That is why a chatbot can "forget" what you said at the start of a very long chat. The model has no memory between requests other than what is placed in the context again.

How big are context windows?

For scale, 128,000 tokens is about 96,000 English words, roughly a long novel. A million tokens can hold a medium-sized codebase or several books. Limits change often, so check the model provider's documentation for current figures, and remember that the maximum output length is usually much smaller than the total window.

Why long context is expensive: the KV cache

When a transformer processes text, each layer stores a key and a value vector for every token so it does not have to recompute them for the next token. This is the KV cache, and it grows linearly with context length.

The KV cache size per token is:

2 (K and V) × layers × KV heads × head dimension × bytes per value

For Llama 3.1 8B (32 layers, 8 KV heads, head dimension 128, FP16):

  • 2 × 32 × 8 × 128 × 2 bytes = 128 KB per token
  • At 128,000 tokens: about 16 GB of KV cache for one conversation

That is on top of about 16 GB for the model weights in FP16. A larger model, or many users at once, multiplies the memory needed. This is a major reason data center GPUs pack so much HBM memory, and why how much VRAM you need for an LLM depends on context length as well as model size.

Why long context is slow: attention

Standard self-attention compares every token with every other token, so the compute for processing a prompt grows roughly with the square of its length. Doubling the prompt can make prefill take far more than twice as long. Techniques that make long context practical include:

  • FlashAttention: computes attention in tiles that fit in fast on-chip memory, cutting memory traffic.
  • Grouped-query attention (GQA): shares key and value heads, shrinking the KV cache.
  • Sliding-window and sparse attention: some layers look only at nearby tokens.
  • Position-encoding extensions: methods that stretch rotary position embeddings (RoPE) to longer sequences than the model saw most in training.
  • KV cache quantization and paging: store the cache in 8-bit or smaller formats and allocate it in blocks.

You can watch how attention connects tokens in our attention mechanism simulator.

Bigger is not always better

A long context window is a maximum, not a guarantee of quality.

  • Lost in the middle: research has shown models are often better at using information at the start and end of a long prompt than in the middle.
  • Effective vs advertised context: a model may accept 1 million tokens but answer reliably only over a smaller range for complex tasks.
  • Cost and latency: every token you send is billed and processed on every request.
  • Distraction: irrelevant text can lower answer quality.

For many applications, retrieving only the most relevant passages with embeddings and RAG beats pasting everything into the prompt.

Practical tips

  • Put the most important instructions at the start and repeat key questions at the end of a long prompt.
  • Remove irrelevant text, boilerplate and duplicated content.
  • Start a new chat when switching topics so old history does not waste tokens.
  • Ask the model to quote the passage it relied on, which makes errors easier to spot.
  • For large document sets, use RAG instead of a giant prompt.
  • When running models locally, set the context length to what you actually need, since it directly controls VRAM use.

Context window vs memory features

Some chat apps advertise "memory" across conversations. That is not a bigger context window: the app saves notes about you and inserts the relevant ones into the context of future chats. The model itself still only sees what fits in its window for each request.

Frequently asked questions

What happens when I exceed the context window?

An API will return an error or truncate input. Chat apps usually drop the oldest messages or summarise them automatically, so the model loses details from earlier in the conversation.

Does the context window include the answer?

Yes. Input and output share the same window. If your prompt uses almost all of it, there is little room left for the reply.

Is a larger context window the same as a smarter model?

No. Context size is how much the model can read at once; intelligence depends on its training, size and architecture. A smaller model with a huge window can still give weaker answers than a stronger model with a shorter window.

How do I set context length when running a model locally?

Tools like Ollama, LM Studio and llama.cpp let you set the context length (for example the num_ctx option in Ollama or -c in llama.cpp). Larger values use more VRAM. See how to run an LLM locally.

Sources and further reading

  • Liu et al., Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts (2023)
  • Su et al., RoFormer: Enhanced Transformer with Rotary Position Embedding (2021)
  • Ainslie et al., GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models (2023)
  • Meta, The Llama 3 Herd of Models (2024)

TITLE: What Is an AI Hallucination? Why ChatGPT Makes Things Up and How to Prevent It
LABEL: GUIDE
EXCERPT: An AI hallucination is when a model confidently states something false or invented. Why language models hallucinate, real examples with real consequences, how to spot them, and the techniques that reduce them.
KEY: An AI hallucination is output from an AI model that sounds confident and plausible but is false, invented or not supported by its sources, such as a fake citation, a wrong statistic or a non-existent product feature. It happens because language models generate the most likely next words rather than looking facts up, and because training and testing have often rewarded guessing over saying "I don't know". Hallucinations can be reduced with retrieval (RAG), citations, better prompts and verification, but not eliminated completely.
content:
Short answer

An AI hallucination is output from an AI model that sounds confident and plausible but is false, invented or not supported by its sources, such as a fake citation, a wrong statistic or a non-existent product feature. It happens because language models generate the most likely next words rather than looking facts up, and because training and testing have often rewarded guessing over saying "I don't know". Hallucinations can be reduced with retrieval (RAG), citations, better prompts and verification, but not eliminated completely.

What a hallucination looks like

Common forms include:

  • Invented sources: citations to papers, court cases or URLs that do not exist.
  • Wrong facts: incorrect dates, numbers, specifications or quotes.
  • Fabricated details: a plausible biography of a person the model knows little about.
  • Unfaithful summaries: a summary that adds claims not in the original document.
  • Made-up code: calls to functions or libraries that do not exist.
  • Image errors: extra fingers or impossible text in generated images are the visual equivalent.

The danger is that hallucinations look exactly like correct answers. The model uses the same confident tone either way.

Why language models hallucinate

They predict text, they do not look it up

A large language model is trained to predict the next token based on patterns in its training data. When it has seen a fact many times, the most likely continuation is usually correct. When a fact is rare, ambiguous or absent, the model still produces the most plausible-sounding continuation, which may be wrong. There is no built-in database it checks against.

Training and testing reward guessing

In 2025, OpenAI researchers argued that hallucinations persist partly because of how models are trained and evaluated. Most benchmarks score answers simply as right or wrong, so a model that guesses gets some points while a model that says "I don't know" gets none. Like a student guessing on a multiple-choice test, models learn that a confident guess scores better than admitting uncertainty. Their proposed fix is to penalise confident errors more than abstentions.

Other causes

  • Knowledge cut-off: the model knows nothing after its training data ends unless connected to search.
  • Compression: billions of facts are squeezed into a fixed number of parameters, so rare details blur.
  • Misleading prompts: a question that assumes something false ("Why did Einstein win two Nobel Prizes?") invites the model to play along.
  • Sampling randomness: higher temperature makes less likely, and sometimes wrong, tokens more probable. See our LLM sampling simulator.
  • Long or noisy context: important information buried in a huge prompt can be missed (see context window).

Real-world consequences

  • Fake legal citations: in 2023 a US federal judge sanctioned two lawyers and their firm $5,000 after they filed a brief citing cases invented by ChatGPT (Mata v. Avianca). Courts in several countries have since seen similar incidents.
  • Customer service: in 2024 a Canadian tribunal ordered Air Canada to honour a refund policy its website chatbot had invented, rejecting the airline's argument that the chatbot was responsible for its own statements.
  • Search answers: AI-generated search summaries have repeated jokes and satire as fact.

The lesson is consistent: organisations are responsible for what their AI tells people.

How to reduce hallucinations

For everyday users

  • Ask for sources and check them. Open the links; do not trust a citation you have not seen.
  • Use search-enabled or document-grounded modes for facts, prices, news and anything recent.
  • Give the model the material. Paste the document and ask it to answer only from that text.
  • Allow uncertainty. Add "If you are not sure, say so" to your prompt.
  • Ask narrow questions instead of broad ones that invite padding.
  • Verify numbers, names, dates and quotes before you publish or act on them.

For developers

  • Retrieval-augmented generation: RAG fetches relevant passages, often with embeddings, and the model answers from them with citations.
  • Lower temperature for factual tasks.
  • Structured output and validation: check generated JSON, code and calculations automatically.
  • Tools: let the model call a calculator, code interpreter, database or search API instead of guessing.
  • Self-checking: have a second pass verify each claim against the sources.
  • Fine-tuning for refusal: training the model to abstain when unsure (see fine-tuning).
  • Evaluation: measure hallucination rates on your own test questions before deploying.

Do bigger or reasoning models hallucinate less?

Generally, newer and larger models hallucinate less on common knowledge, and models that can search the web make fewer factual errors on current events. But no model is hallucination-free. Some reasoning models have scored worse on certain factual benchmarks than their predecessors, because longer chains of reasoning create more chances to introduce an unsupported claim. Treat every model as a fast, helpful assistant whose work still needs checking.

Is hallucination always bad?

In creative work, the same ability to generate plausible new material is the point: story ideas, brainstorming, fictional worlds and design concepts. The problem is only when invented content is presented, or taken, as fact.

Frequently asked questions

Why is it called a hallucination?

The term borrows from psychology, where a hallucination is a perception of something not present. Some researchers prefer "confabulation", meaning confidently filling gaps with invented details, which describes the behaviour more precisely.

Can AI hallucinations be completely eliminated?

Not with current language model designs. Because they generate text from probabilities, there is always some chance of a plausible but wrong output. Grounding, tools and verification can make them rare in specific applications.

How often do chatbots hallucinate?

It depends heavily on the model, the task and whether it has access to sources. Rates are low for well-known facts and summarising a provided document, and much higher for obscure facts, citations and questions about little-known people.

Does RAG stop hallucinations?

It reduces them significantly by giving the model the right information, but the model can still misread or misquote a source. Good RAG systems show citations so users can check.

Sources and further reading

  • Kalai et al., Why Language Models Hallucinate (OpenAI, 2025)
  • Ji et al., Survey of Hallucination in Natural Language Generation (2022)
  • Lewis et al., Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks (2020)
  • American Bar Association, Use of ChatGPT for research leads to sanctions for bogus cases (2023)

TITLE: What Is Fine-Tuning in AI? LoRA, QLoRA and When to Fine-Tune vs Use RAG
LABEL: GUIDE
EXCERPT: Fine-tuning further trains a pre-trained AI model on your own examples so it follows a format, style or task better. How it works, full fine-tuning vs LoRA and QLoRA, how much GPU memory you need, and when RAG or prompting is the better choice.
KEY: Fine-tuning means taking a model that has already been pre-trained on a huge general dataset and training it a little more on a smaller, specific dataset so it gets better at a particular task, style or format. Modern methods such as LoRA and QLoRA train only a tiny set of extra weights, so a 7B or 8B model can be fine-tuned on a single 16 to 24 GB GPU. Fine-tuning is best for teaching behaviour and format; for adding up-to-date facts, RAG is usually the better tool.
content:
Short answer

Fine-tuning means taking a model that has already been pre-trained on a huge general dataset and training it a little more on a smaller, specific dataset so it gets better at a particular task, style or format. Modern methods such as LoRA and QLoRA train only a tiny set of extra weights, so a 7B or 8B model can be fine-tuned on a single 16 to 24 GB GPU. Fine-tuning is best for teaching behaviour and format; for adding up-to-date facts, RAG is usually the better tool.

How fine-tuning fits into model training

Most language models go through several stages:

1. Pre-training: the model learns language and general knowledge by predicting the next token over trillions of tokens. This is the expensive part (see AI training vs inference). 2. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT): the model is trained on examples of prompts and ideal responses, which turns a raw text predictor into a helpful assistant. 3. Preference tuning: methods such as RLHF (reinforcement learning from human feedback) or DPO (direct preference optimization) teach the model which of two answers people prefer.

When companies and developers talk about fine-tuning, they usually mean doing step 2, and sometimes step 3, again on their own data, starting from an existing open model or through a provider's fine-tuning API.

What fine-tuning is good for

  • Consistent format: always returning valid JSON, a specific report layout or a fixed tone.
  • Domain style and terminology: legal drafting, medical coding conventions, a brand voice.
  • Narrow tasks: classification, extraction, routing or tagging, where a small fine-tuned model can match a much larger general model.
  • Shorter prompts: behaviour you would otherwise describe in a long system prompt gets built into the model, saving tokens.
  • Smaller, cheaper models: fine-tuning a small model on outputs from a large one (distillation) cuts serving costs.

What fine-tuning is not good for

  • Adding fresh facts: knowledge learned by fine-tuning is hard to update and the model may still hallucinate details. Use RAG for documents, prices and anything that changes.
  • Citing sources: a fine-tuned model cannot point to where a fact came from.
  • Fixing a weak base model: fine-tuning sharpens existing abilities more than it creates new ones.

Fine-tuning vs RAG vs prompt engineering

A practical order is: try better prompts first, add RAG if the model lacks knowledge, and fine-tune when you need consistent behaviour that prompting cannot deliver. Many production systems combine RAG and fine-tuning.

Full fine-tuning vs parameter-efficient fine-tuning

Full fine-tuning

All of the model's weights are updated. This gives the most control but needs the same memory as training: about 16 bytes per parameter with mixed precision and the Adam optimizer, so a 7B model needs over 100 GB plus activations. That means several data center GPUs, and you must store a full new copy of the model for every fine-tune.

LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation)

LoRA freezes the original weights and adds small trainable matrices to selected layers. Instead of updating a large weight matrix directly, it learns two thin matrices whose product represents the change. The LoRA paper reported cutting the number of trainable parameters for GPT-3 by 10,000 times and GPU memory needs by about 3 times, with quality on par with full fine-tuning. The resulting "adapter" is often only tens or hundreds of megabytes and can be swapped on and off the base model.

QLoRA

QLoRA goes further by loading the frozen base model in 4-bit precision and training LoRA adapters on top. Its authors fine-tuned a 65-billion-parameter model on a single 48 GB GPU. QLoRA is the most common way hobbyists and small teams fine-tune models today. For more on 4-bit formats, see LLM quantization.

How much GPU memory do you need?

Rough guide for fine-tuning language models (exact needs depend on sequence length, batch size and settings):

A 24 GB card such as the RTX 4090 or RTX 5090 covers most hobby fine-tuning; see the best GPU for local LLMs. For bigger jobs, renting an H100 or A100 by the hour is usually cheaper than buying; check today's rates in our GPU cloud price tracker.

The fine-tuning process, step by step

1. Define the task and success metric. What exactly should improve, and how will you measure it? 2. Collect examples. Hundreds to a few thousand high-quality prompt-response pairs often beat a larger, messy dataset. 3. Format the data in the chat template your base model expects. 4. Choose a base model that already does reasonably well on the task. 5. Train with a library such as Hugging Face TRL and PEFT, Unsloth or Axolotl, or with a provider's fine-tuning API. 6. Evaluate on held-out examples the model never saw, and compare against the base model with a good prompt. 7. Deploy by merging the adapter or loading it at inference time, and keep monitoring.

Risks to watch

  • Overfitting: the model memorises training examples and generalises poorly.
  • Catastrophic forgetting: it gets worse at things it used to do well.
  • Safety regression: research has shown fine-tuning can weaken a model's safety training, even with harmless data, so re-test safety behaviour.
  • Licences: check the base model's licence allows your use.

Frequently asked questions

How many examples do I need to fine-tune?

For format and style, a few hundred good examples can be enough. Complex tasks may need thousands. Quality and consistency matter more than volume.

Can I fine-tune ChatGPT or Claude?

OpenAI offers fine-tuning for several of its models through its API, and some providers offer fine-tuning on their cloud platforms. Open-weight models such as Llama, Mistral, Qwen and Gemma can be fine-tuned on your own hardware.

Is fine-tuning the same as training from scratch?

No. Training from scratch builds all of a model's knowledge from random weights and costs millions of dollars for large models. Fine-tuning starts from a capable model and adjusts it, usually in hours.

Does fine-tuning make a model smarter?

It makes a model better at the specific task you trained it on. It rarely improves general reasoning and can sometimes reduce performance on unrelated tasks.

Sources and further reading

  • Hu et al., LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models (2021)
  • Dettmers et al., QLoRA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs (2023)
  • Ouyang et al., Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback (InstructGPT, 2022)
  • Rafailov et al., Direct Preference Optimization (2023)
  • Qi et al., Fine-tuning Aligned Language Models Compromises Safety (2023)
  • Hugging Face, PEFT documentation

TITLE: What Is Generative AI? How It Works, Examples and Limits (Beginner Guide)
LABEL: GUIDE
EXCERPT: Generative AI creates new text, images, code, audio and video from a prompt. A plain-English guide to how it works, the main model types (LLMs, diffusion, GANs), real examples, the hardware behind it and its limits.
KEY: Generative AI is artificial intelligence that creates new content (text, images, code, audio or video) instead of only classifying or predicting. It learns the patterns in huge amounts of training data and then produces new output that follows those patterns when you give it a prompt. ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini generate text with large language models; Midjourney, Stable Diffusion and FLUX generate images with diffusion models. All of them run on GPUs or other AI accelerators.
content:
Short answer

Generative AI is artificial intelligence that creates new content (text, images, code, audio or video) instead of only classifying or predicting. It learns the patterns in huge amounts of training data and then produces new output that follows those patterns when you give it a prompt. ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini generate text with large language models; Midjourney, Stable Diffusion and FLUX generate images with diffusion models. All of them run on GPUs or other AI accelerators.

Generative AI in one sentence

Traditional AI answers questions like "is this email spam?" or "what will sales be next month?". Generative AI answers "write me an email", "draw a cat in a spacesuit" or "turn this text into speech". It produces something that did not exist before.

That shift is why generative AI exploded after OpenAI released ChatGPT on November 30, 2022. Anyone could type a request in plain language and get a useful result back in seconds.

How generative AI works

Every generative model follows the same three-step idea:

1. Learn from data. During training, a neural network with billions of adjustable numbers (parameters) is shown enormous amounts of text, images or audio. It slowly adjusts its parameters to capture the statistical patterns in that data. 2. Take a prompt. You describe what you want. The prompt is converted into numbers the model can process, such as tokens for text. 3. Generate step by step. The model produces output a piece at a time. A language model predicts the next token again and again; an image model starts from random noise and removes it step by step until a picture appears.

The model is not copying and pasting from a database. It is sampling new output from the patterns it learned, which is why the same prompt can give a different answer every time and why it can sometimes produce confident errors (see AI hallucinations).

The main types of generative AI models

Large language models

LLMs are built on the transformer architecture, introduced by Google researchers in 2017. They are trained to predict the next token in trillions of words of text. That simple goal, at huge scale, produces models that can write, summarise, translate, reason through problems and write code. Our guide What is an LLM? covers them in depth, and How does ChatGPT work? walks through a real product.

Diffusion models

Diffusion models generate images by learning to reverse a noising process. During training, images are gradually corrupted with random noise and the model learns to predict and remove that noise. To create a new image it starts from pure noise and denoises it over 20 to 50 steps, guided by your text prompt. Stable Diffusion made this practical on consumer GPUs in 2022 by working in a compressed "latent" space rather than on full-size pixels. If you want to run these models yourself, see the best GPU for Stable Diffusion.

GANs

Generative adversarial networks, introduced in 2014, pit two networks against each other: a generator makes fake samples and a discriminator tries to spot them. GANs produced the first photorealistic AI faces, but diffusion models have largely replaced them for image generation because they are easier to train and more controllable.

What generative AI is used for

  • Writing and editing: drafts, emails, summaries, translation and rewriting.
  • Coding: code completion, explaining code, writing tests and fixing bugs.
  • Search and question answering: chat assistants that answer from documents using RAG.
  • Images and design: concept art, product mock-ups, marketing visuals and photo editing.
  • Video and audio: short video clips, voice-overs, dubbing and music.
  • Agents: AI agents that plan multi-step tasks and use tools such as a browser or a code interpreter.
  • Science: protein structure and drug discovery models apply the same ideas to molecules.

McKinsey estimated that generative AI could add the equivalent of $2.6 trillion to $4.4 trillion to the global economy every year across the use cases it analysed.

Generative AI vs traditional AI

Both are part of machine learning. For how the terms fit together, read AI vs machine learning vs deep learning.

The hardware behind generative AI

Generative AI is extremely compute-hungry, which is why NVIDIA GPUs became some of the most sought-after products in the world.

  • Training a frontier model uses thousands or tens of thousands of GPUs in a GPU cluster for weeks or months. Meta trained Llama 3.1 405B on up to 16,000 H100 GPUs.
  • Running (inference) a model needs enough VRAM to hold its weights and enough memory bandwidth to read them for every token it generates.
  • Tensor cores inside modern GPUs do the matrix multiplications that make up almost all of the work. See What is a tensor core?.

You can run smaller generative models on your own PC: see how to run an LLM locally. For larger jobs, renting is often cheaper; our GPU cloud price tracker compares daily rental prices.

Limitations and risks

  • Hallucinations: models can state false information confidently.
  • Bias: outputs can reflect biases in the training data.
  • Copyright and data questions: several lawsuits are testing whether training on copyrighted material is lawful.
  • Misuse: deepfakes, scams and spam become cheaper to produce.
  • Cost and energy: large models need AI data centers that use significant electricity.
  • Knowledge cut-off: a model only knows what was in its training data unless it is connected to search or documents.

Frequently asked questions

Is ChatGPT generative AI?

Yes. ChatGPT is a chat application built on OpenAI's GPT family of large language models, which are generative models that produce text one token at a time.

What is the difference between AI and generative AI?

AI is the whole field of making computers perform tasks that need intelligence. Generative AI is the subset that creates new content. A spam filter is AI but not generative; a chatbot that writes replies is generative AI.

Can generative AI think?

Generative models do not think the way people do. They produce output by predicting likely continuations based on patterns learned in training. Newer "reasoning" models generate step-by-step working before answering, which improves accuracy on maths and logic, but they can still make basic mistakes.

Do I need a powerful computer to use generative AI?

Not to use it: chat apps and image tools run in the cloud. To run models on your own computer, a GPU with 8 to 16 GB of VRAM handles small language models and most image models. See how much VRAM you need for an LLM.

Sources and further reading

  • Goodfellow et al., Generative Adversarial Networks (2014)
  • Vaswani et al., Attention Is All You Need (2017)
  • Ho et al., Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (2020)
  • Rombach et al., High-Resolution Image Synthesis with Latent Diffusion Models (2021)
  • McKinsey, The economic potential of generative AI (2023)

TITLE: What Is Mixture of Experts (MoE)? How Sparse AI Models Work and What They Mean for GPUs
LABEL: EXPLAINER
EXCERPT: Mixture of experts (MoE) models split their layers into many expert networks and use only a few per token. How routing works, total vs active parameters, real examples like Mixtral, DeepSeek-V3, Llama 4 and gpt-oss, and the memory and interconnect demands on hardware.
KEY: A mixture of experts (MoE) model replaces some of a neural network's layers with many smaller "expert" sub-networks plus a router that sends each token to only a few of them. The model can have a very large total parameter count while using only a small fraction, the active parameters, for each token. DeepSeek-V3, for example, has 671 billion parameters but activates about 37 billion per token. MoE makes large models faster and cheaper to run per token, but all experts must still fit in memory, which makes VRAM capacity and GPU interconnect the main hardware challenges.
content:
Short answer

A mixture of experts (MoE) model replaces some of a neural network's layers with many smaller "expert" sub-networks plus a router that sends each token to only a few of them. The model can have a very large total parameter count while using only a small fraction, the active parameters, for each token. DeepSeek-V3, for example, has 671 billion parameters but activates about 37 billion per token. MoE makes large models faster and cheaper to run per token, but all experts must still fit in memory, which makes VRAM capacity and GPU interconnect the main hardware challenges.

The idea in plain English

Imagine a hospital. Instead of one doctor who must know everything, there are many specialists and a receptionist who sends each patient to the two most suitable ones. The hospital as a whole knows a lot, but each patient only takes up the time of two doctors.

An MoE model works the same way. The "receptionist" is a small router network, the "specialists" are expert networks, and each "patient" is a token.

How MoE works inside a transformer

A standard transformer layer has two main parts: an attention block and a feed-forward network (FFN). The FFN holds most of the parameters. In an MoE model:

1. The single FFN is replaced by many expert FFNs (for example 8, 64, 128 or 256). 2. For each token, a router computes a score for every expert. 3. The token is sent to the top-k experts, usually 1, 2 or 8. 4. The outputs of the chosen experts are combined, weighted by the router scores.

Attention layers are usually shared by all tokens. Some designs also include one or more shared experts that every token uses, alongside the routed ones.

Because only k experts run for each token, the compute per token depends on the active parameters, not the total.

Total vs active parameters: real examples

Many frontier models are also widely believed to use MoE, though most closed-model developers do not publish their architectures.

Why MoE is popular

  • More knowledge for the same compute: a model with 400B total parameters can store far more than a 17B dense model, while costing roughly the same compute per token.
  • Cheaper training: for a fixed training compute budget, MoE models typically reach better quality than dense models.
  • Faster generation: token generation is limited by how many bytes of weights must be read from memory per token. With MoE, only active experts' weights are read, so decode can be much faster than a dense model of the same total size. See prefill vs decode.

The catch: memory and communication

All experts must live in memory

Even though only a few experts run per token, any expert could be chosen for the next token, so all of them must be loaded in GPU memory (or very fast memory nearby). A 671B-parameter model needs about 671 GB in FP8, or roughly 335 GB in 4-bit, before the KV cache. That is why MoE models favour GPUs with large HBM capacity, such as the H200 (141 GB) and B200 (180 GB class), and multi-GPU servers.

For local use, MoE is a mixed blessing: a large MoE model needs lots of VRAM or system RAM, but once loaded it runs fast because few parameters are read per token. This is why MoE models are popular on Apple Silicon Macs with large unified memory and why tools like llama.cpp can offload experts to system RAM. gpt-oss-120b was designed to run on a single 80 GB GPU using 4-bit MXFP4 weights.

Experts are spread across GPUs

Large MoE models use expert parallelism: different GPUs hold different experts. Every layer, tokens must be sent to whichever GPUs hold their chosen experts and the results sent back. This all-to-all communication is heavy, so MoE performance depends strongly on interconnect bandwidth. NVIDIA's NVLink and NVSwitch and rack-scale systems like the GB200 NVL72, which link 72 GPUs in one NVLink domain, are well suited to this workload.

Load balancing

If the router sends most tokens to a few popular experts, those GPUs become bottlenecks while others sit idle. Training uses extra techniques, such as auxiliary balancing losses or the bias-based balancing used in DeepSeek-V3, to spread tokens evenly.

MoE vs dense models

A short history

  • 1991: Jacobs, Jordan, Nowlan and Hinton propose "adaptive mixtures of local experts".
  • 2017: Google's Noam Shazeer and colleagues scale MoE layers to over 100 billion parameters in an LSTM model with a sparsely gated MoE layer.
  • 2021: Google's Switch Transformer routes each token to a single expert and scales to over a trillion parameters.
  • 2023 to 2025: Mixtral, DeepSeek-V2 and V3, Qwen MoE models, Llama 4 and gpt-oss bring MoE into the mainstream of open models.

Frequently asked questions

Are the experts specialised in topics like maths or history?

Not in a neat, human-readable way. Studies of models like Mixtral found experts tend to specialise more in token types and syntax than in subject areas. The specialisation is learned automatically and is hard to interpret.

Is an MoE model with 400B parameters as smart as a 400B dense model?

Usually not. An MoE model typically performs better than a dense model with the same number of active parameters, but somewhat below a dense model with the same total parameters. Its advantage is efficiency.

Can I run an MoE model on my PC?

Smaller ones, yes. gpt-oss-20b and Qwen's smaller MoE models run on GPUs with 16 GB or more, and quantized versions of larger MoE models can run on high-memory Macs or PCs with lots of system RAM. See how to run an LLM locally and how much VRAM you need.

Why does MoE matter for GPU buyers?

It shifts the bottleneck from compute towards memory capacity and interconnect. That is one reason newer data center GPUs keep adding HBM and NVLink bandwidth, and why prices for high-memory GPUs remain strong; see our GPU cloud price tracker.
